edition.subtitle: Some people forget almost nothing. It turns out that is not the advantage it sounds like.

news.source: Science News, September 2026; Gabrielle Principe, The Conversation, May 2026.
news.text: Memory does not record experience — it reconstructs it at the moment of recall, assembled from fragments filtered by present knowledge, mood, and goals. For decades, forgetting was treated as a passive breakdown of that system: information wearing away with time. Research summarized in Science News's September 2026 cover story, drawing on work by neurologist Scott A. Small of Columbia University and memory researcher Gabrielle Principe of the College of Charleston, finds instead that forgetting runs on its own dedicated neurobiological machinery.

body: Ask someone what they were doing on an ordinary Tuesday eleven years ago and almost nobody can answer. What they produce instead, if pressed, is a reconstruction built from what usually happens on Tuesdays, filled in with plausible detail, offered with more confidence than it deserves. Retrieval assembles a version of the past that fits the moment it's being asked for, which is also why the same memory comes back slightly different a year later.

For most of the history of neuroscience, the assumption was that whatever didn't survive this rebuilding had simply worn out — a passive failure, entropy acting on a fragile system. The newer findings overturn that. Forgetting runs on its own circuitry, its own dedicated molecular pathways, active and specific in what it targets. The system clears fine-grained detail and keeps whatever generalizes.

This matters because a detail, once cleared, stops competing. A method learned under one set of conditions can sit in the same neural territory as a method learned under different ones, and the two will interfere with each other unless something makes room. Active forgetting weakens the old pattern's pull enough that a new one can form without having to out-compete it every time it's needed. What comes back afterward is rebuilt to fit the present case — usually more useful than the original would have been.

The same mechanism appears to protect something less mechanical than skill. People who dwell least on a humiliation, a failure, an old grievance, are not necessarily people with weaker memories. They may simply have more efficient active forgetting — the emotional charge stripped from the detail faster, so the event stops being available at full intensity every time something reminds them of it.

The clearest evidence for what this buys comes from people who don't have it. A small number of individuals have Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory: ask them about a specific day fifteen or twenty years back, an ordinary Wednesday with no reason to be remembered, and they will tell you, in detail, what happened. It sounds like an advantage until they describe living with it. The failures don't fade. The embarrassments stay as sharp on the thousandth recall as on the first. Several describe the condition as exhausting, because no version of the past available to them has been allowed to soften.
